pages.text: The set turns at 1800 rev/min with nothing connected. Its voltage follows the field current along the open-circuit curve. It climbs in step at first. Then it bends over at a knee as the iron saturates.

pages.name: Double the field
pages.task: With nothing connected, the field current doubles from 100% to 200%. The curve marks 440 V at 100% and 555 V at 200%. How many times higher is the voltage now?
pages.why: 555 ÷ 440 = 1.26. The field current doubled, but the flux did not. The iron is saturating, so the voltage rose by only 26%.

pages.task: In a brushless set, which winding does the AVR's output feed?
pages.why: The AVR sits off the shaft. It feeds the exciter's fixed field, which needs no brushes. The exciter's turning coils and the diodes then carry a much bigger current into the main field.

pages.alt: A brushless generator set drawn side-on along one shaft turning at 1800 rev/min: the PMG, the exciter with its fixed field and turning coils, the diodes on the shaft, and the main field inside the stator. The output runs to the load. The AVR is off. It senses the output, takes its power from the output, by the shunt lead, and feeds the exciter's fixed field. The exciter's field bars and the main field's bar stand at their 100% ticks. The open-circuit curve: the voltage the set makes inside, 0 to 600 V, against the field current, 0 to 200%. It climbs steeply, then bends over at a knee. A dot marks the present field current on the curve, and a ring below it marks the voltage at the board. The line between them is the drop the load causes inside the machine. A dashed line marks the 440 V set point. A trace of the voltage at the board against time, newest at the right, with the 440 V set point dashed. It ends below the set point, after a change a few seconds ago.
pages.name: A load pulls it down
pages.text: The AVR is off and the field is held at 100%. The load's current drops voltage inside the machine. So a 50% load pulls the voltage down from 440 V to 390 V. It stays there.

pages.name: Field held, more load
pages.task: The AVR is off and the field is held at 100%. The load goes from 0% to 80%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. What voltage reaches the board?
pages.why: 80% of load drops 80 V. The field has not moved, so the curve still gives 440 V inside. So 440 − 80 = 360 V reaches the board. It stays there.

The output runs to the load. The AVR is on. It senses the output, takes its power from the output, by the shunt lead, and feeds the exciter's fixed field. The exciter's field bars and the main field's bar stand past their 100% ticks. The open-circuit curve: the voltage the set makes inside, 0 to 600 V, against the field current, 0 to 200%. It climbs steeply, then bends over at a knee. A dot marks the present field current on the curve, and a ring below it marks the voltage at the board. The line between them is the drop the load causes inside the machine. A dashed line marks the 440 V set point. A trace of the voltage at the board against time, newest at the right, with the 440 V set point dashed. It ends on the set point, after a change a few seconds ago.
pages.name: The AVR brings it back
pages.text: With the AVR on, a 50% load dips the voltage towards 390 V at first. The AVR compares the output with its 440 V set point and raises the exciter's field. The load's drop is 50 V, so the set must make 490 V inside. The main field climbs to 125%, and the output returns to 440 V.

The line between them is the drop the load causes inside the machine. A dashed line marks the 440 V set point. A trace of the voltage at the board against time, newest at the right, with the 440 V set point dashed. It ends on the set point, after a change a few seconds ago.
pages.name: Full load
pages.task: The AVR holds 440 V at 50% load with the field at 125%. The load rises to 100%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. The curve marks 490 V at 125%, 520 V at 150% and 540 V at 175%. What field current does the AVR settle at?
pages.why: At 100% load the drop is 100 V. So the set must make 440 + 100 = 540 V inside. The curve gives 540 V at 175%. The first half of the load took 25% more field. The second half took 50%. The dot is now climbing past the knee.

pages.task: A short circuit on the board pulls the set's output voltage close to zero. Which AVR supply can keep the field up?
pages.why: The PMG takes its power from the shaft, not from the output. So the AVR can keep the exciter's field up through the fault. A shunt-fed AVR loses its power with the output. So the field and the fault current die away. The protection needs that current to last long enough to clear the fault.

pages.name: The load trips
pages.task: The AVR holds 440 V at 50% load, so the field sits at 125%. The load trips off. The curve marks 490 V at 125%. What is the voltage in the instant before the AVR acts?
pages.why: The field is still at 125%, so the curve gives 490 V inside. With no load there is no drop. So the output jumps to 490 V. Then the AVR lowers the field until the board reads 440 V again.

pages.name: A light load
pages.task: The AVR is on and the load rises from 0% to 20%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. The curve runs straight from 440 V at 100% to 490 V at 125%. What field current does the AVR settle at?
pages.why: The drop is 20 V, so the set must make 460 V inside. That is 20 V of the 50 V between 100% and 125%. So the field rises 20 ÷ 50 × 25 = 10%, to 110%.
